News.title: Tragic final call of man, 21, before he was knifed to death at UK beauty spot as pal heard screams when fight broke out
News.content:
A MAN who was knifed to death at a UK beauty spot was heard screaming on the phone to his pal as a brutal fight broke out.

Film student Finbar Sullivan, 21, tragically died following an attack at Primrose Hill, North London on Tuesday evening.





Cops rushed to the scene, having received reports of a fight at around 6.40pm, where they discovered Finbar with stab wounds.

He was sadly pronounced dead at the scene, with his heartbroken dad Christopher describing it as “the worst tragedy I could ever imagine”.

Now, one of his closest pals has paid an emotional tribute to his young friend – who he spoke with on the phone just moments before his death.

The man, who asked not to be named, said: “I was on the phone when it happened.

“I was on the phone at 6.39pm and he was like ‘Yo, me and a few friends are gonna go get a Lime bike down to grab some drinks’.

“And then the phone went quiet for like 30 seconds.

“And it sort of sounded like it was muted, and then it went unmute, and I just hear screaming, like heavy breathing and that, and then I just said, ‘Fin, call me back when you can’, and hung up because I was just scared, I didn’t know what to do.



“I thought maybe an altercation, hopefully he’s run off and he’s all good. I tried to call and message him after.”

Speaking at a shrine of flowers and candles near to where the young student was killed, the friend described being with Finbar as “a breath of fresh air”.

He said: “He was a brilliant man, a constant hard worker. He never stopped working. He always said, live every day like it is your last. That was his favourite quote.

“To spend time with him was a breath of fresh air. He was always making jokes and making sure everyone was feeling good.”

Finbar was a music video director for rap and drill artists in the UK under the name “Sully Shot It”.



Shocking video footage circulating on social media seems to show a knife fight breaking out in the park.

Finbar’s dad Christopher told how his son had gone up to the hill to do some filming with a new camera before his tragic death.

The 65-year-old also revealed Finbar had been with his friend who bravely tried to protect him and was himself attacked in the process.



The Metropolitan Police said no arrests have so far been made.

Cops are now pleading for a key witness to come forward – a young woman or teenager – to help solve the tragic case.

The woman was captured on film recording a fight in the park shortly before the murder.

In a statement, cops said: “The footage she filmed is vital to ongoing enquiries and will help officers piece together the sequence of events.”

She has not committed any offences and is being treated as a significant witness.



Footage shows her wearing a pink top, blue denim shorts and black trainers.

Detective Inspector Andy Griffin, who is leading the investigation, said: “My team continues to pursue several urgent lines of enquiry to establish why Fin tragically lost his life.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I believe this woman’s account of events, as well as the video she captured, will provide vital evidence.

“To reiterate, she has not committed any offence but we are urging her, or anyone who may know her, to come forward and assist our investigation. We need to speak to her as soon as possible.”

News.title: Moment car drives at crowd gathered in park as yobs smash windows & lob projectiles in night of mayhem
News.content:
THIS is the moment a car drives at a crowd gathered in a park, as yobs smash in windows and lob projectiles in a night of chaos.

Shocking footage shows a car reversing into a crowd of youths gathered late at night.





The terrifying scenes are understood to have unfolded at Beckenham Place Park in south London on Wednesday.

The mob is seen scattering but then pounding at the windows of a different vehicle nearby.

They kick in windows and film as the driver cowers and tries to get away, but is hemmed in by the amount of cars.

Several of the crowd seem to be inhaling from balloons and laughing.

The vehicle eventually manages to drive off, with the passenger door hanging open.

In a different clip, a car is surrounded by the mob as objects are lobbed over their heads.

The Met Police said in a statement: “We recognise the concern this has caused for local residents and officers are working at pace to identify and locate those seen in the videos.

“Local people can expect to see an increased police presence in the area over the coming days.



“We’d encourage anyone with information to get in touch with us so we can pursue every possible line of enquiry.”

It comes after feral youths sparked chaos in UK cities, storming shops and terrifying families during so called “linkups” fuelled by social media.

Groups of marauding teens tore through Clapham High Street, London, and in Birmingham at the beginning of the month.

The incidents saw the Marks and Spencer in Clapham stormed along with several other stores after teens gathered in the area en masse.



Shops including Waitrose, Sainsbury’s and McDonald’s were forced to close early as cops fought to bring the chaotic situation under control.

Thinus Keeve, retail director at M&S, has slammed London’s Mayor for failing to tackle crime in the capital.

He wrote in The Telegraph: “I keep hearing crime is falling, especially in London.

“Something none of us believes, and very few people working in retail would see.



“Without a Government seriously cracking down on crime and a Mayor that prioritises effective policing, we are powerless.”

Two teen girls aged 16 and one 15-year-old were arrested in London on suspicion of shoplifting and assault after the “linkups”. All three have since been bailed.

Flailing cops were heavily outnumbered by the vast swathes of youths unleashing havoc – as they desperately tried to chase the youngsters away.

The Met Police warned teens: “just because you have not been arrested does not mean you will not be.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Officers have set up a policing plan to prevent any future chaos after Clapham High Street was overrun on two occasions.



The Met added that social media companies must play their part in preventing the anti-social events, which the force said were being fuelled by social media platforms.

News.title: Woman, 49, killed by decaying tree after huge branch fell on her as she took evening stroll with husband
News.content:
TRAGIC WALK Woman, 49, killed by decaying tree after huge branch fell on her as she took evening stroll with husband

A WOMAN was killed by a decaying tree after a huge branch fell on her as she took an evening stroll with her husband, an inquest heard.

Jen Higgins, 49, had no time to react as the mature beech tree toppled across the road and on to the pavement on the other side.





Her husband Gawen told Manchester Coroners’ Court his wife “took the full force” of the falling branch during the horror on August 30 last year.

Tragically, Jen could not be saved and was declared dead at the scene in Manchester.

Her cause of death was given as multiple traumatic chest injuries caused by blunt force trauma.

An inquest heard the tree, situated in the garden of a home, had been pruned 15 to 20 years previously and as a result had developed unseen decay, which left the wood “almost like tissue paper”.

Jen and Gawith were walking with another couple when they heard a “loud crack” as a third of the canopy of the tree fell away.

Gawith, who was left with bruising and scratching, said: “We had no time to take any kind of evasive action. It was extremely sudden with no warning.”

Noel Nugent, a senior arboricultural officer at Manchester council, told the court the tree was not covered by a Tree Preservation Order and was not in a conservation area.

He said it had suffered “significant decay’ but that this would not have been “visible”.



Recording a verdict of accidental death, assistant coroner Jennifer Swift said there was no requirement for the tree owners to look for any decay or have it inspected.

She added: “To me this is nothing short of a tragic, devastating accident that occurred that day.”

Jen ran Northern Quarter-based PR firm Carousel with her husband.

Paying tribute previously, her family said: “The family of Jen Higgins are heartbroken to confirm she lost her life in a sudden and tragic accident.

“She was a beloved wife, daughter, sister, daughter-in-law, and aunt – a vibrant and supportive friend to many; and a dynamic and widely respected member of the Manchester business community.



“You will no doubt empathise with the deep and profound shock we are feeling at this moment and ask for privacy while we grieve. A further statement will be issued when we feel able.”

News.title: How fatal ticking time bomb disease claimed the lives of stars Eric Dane & Michael Campbell – are you at risk?
News.content:
TO the outside world, actors Michael Campbell and Eric Dane were healthy men with bright futures – but the ticking time bomb of a fatal disease lurked inside.

It is estimated that one in 300 people is at risk of suffering from that very same incurable disease. Here, The Sun takes a look at the heartbreaking condition and why the cause is still baffling experts.



Motor Neurone Disease (MND) affects the brain and spinal cord nerves, leading to vital muscles wasting away.

Whether someone might develop the fatal disease or not is far from an exact science.



Increased research into this mysterious illness appears to be leading to a greater understanding of what causes MND, also referred to as ALS in the United States.

Mutations in particular genes, such as the C9ORF72 one, exposure to heavy metals like mercury and, most surprisingly, lots of exercise have all been put forward as possible causes.

There is a strong fear that head injuries sustained while playing rugby and football are leading to MND.

That follows high-profile cases involving rugby league star Rob Burrow, rugby union legend Lewis Moody and former Ipswich Town striker Marcus Stewart.

We think it’s a combination of the genetic makeup of the person, and their lifestyle Professor Pam Shaw

It is most likely that, rather than being a direct cause, a sporting injury could be a trigger for a faulty gene.



MND expert Professor Dame Pam Shaw, director of Sheffield Institute for Translational Neuroscience, said: “Clearly, most athletes don’t develop MND. We think it’s a combination of the genetic makeup of the person and their lifestyle.”

Here we look at the MND risk factors:

Genetics

Game of Thrones and Blue Lights actor Michael Campbell was one of the ten per cent of sufferers who inherited the killer disease.

It was revealed this week that the 35-year-old Northern Irishman had died in a hospice after being diagnosed with MND just over three years ago.

He had a very rare fault in his FUS gene, which only affects 300 people globally.



Michael’s father also died from MND.

Some people with a family history of the disease are now having genetic tests to see if they have a potentially faulty version of the C9ORF72 gene, which is associated with the condition.

A mother-of-three called Rose, told The Sunday Telegraph, how she took a genetic test in 2023 after her mother Ruby was diagnosed with MND.

Rose, 32, came back as C9ORF72-positive and quit her job in order to spend more time with her young children while she can.

She didn’t want to wait until symptoms developed, because many patients die within two years of seeing the first signs.



She said: “You can walk about feeling quite a loss for yourself and waste years of your life in limbo, in grief.

“But despite all the sadness that’s happened in my life in the last few years, the results have really held me together because it means I have a choice in how I live now.”

Research suggests that about 40 per cent of people with MND whose relatives also had the condition had a faulty C9ORF72 gene.

Everyone has the C9ORF72 gene, but only one in 635 has a mutation.

Sporty lifestyle

One of the most moving images of recent years was when rugby star Kevin Sinfield carried his pal Rob Burrow over the finish line of the Leeds Marathon.



Former Leeds Rhinos player Rob, whose condition was not hereditary, died aged 41 in June 2024, just over four years after finding out he had MND.

Research of 400 former Scottish rugby players by the University of Glasgow in 2022 found that they had an increased risk of developing the condition.

The latest big-name rugby star to be diagnosed with MND is Lewis Moody, 47, who played 71 times for England.

Moreover, analysis of 4,000 death certificates of professional footballers by a team at King’s College discovered a rate of MND higher than in the general population.

There are suggestions that brain injuries, which come from contact sports, are a major factor.



But Moody, knowing what he knows now, would still play the game, saying: “I absolutely loved it.”

It isn’t just contact sports, though, that are associated with MND.

Professor Shaw noticed that most of her patients had lived fit and healthy lives.



She studied two twins, who had the C9ORF72 gene.

Professor Shaw said: “One twin was an ‘iron man’ – he was going to the gym every day and doing triathlon-type things, and he developed MND in his 30s, and died.

“His identical twin was the complete opposite – a sedentary person who didn’t do any exercise, and 12 years later, he was fine.”

Age and gender

Motor Neurone Disease affects up to 5,000 adults in the United Kingdom at any one time – but it is far more prevalent in people aged over 50.

It also appears to be more common in men.



There are 1.5 males diagnosed with MND for every one woman with the condition.

Statistics should not be relied upon, because the odds can be unfair.

Barbara Shooter, 69, from South London, revealed how both she and her husband Adrian were both diagnosed with MND.

Adrian no longer wanted to live with the illness, where you can feel every itch but can’t move and eventually can’t swallow, so he went to Switzerland to end his life in 2022, aged 74.

At the end of last year, Barbara also discovered she had the disease.



She said: “I’ve seen it up so close and it’s a messy, brutal, nasty, vile disease. I know, I’ve been there. I’ve lived it with Adrian.

“I was thinking: ‘God, anything but MND, please. Anything.’ But, you know, here we are. I’ve got it.”

Most people die within two years of being diagnosed with MND, but scientist Stephen Hawking survived for 55 years before dying aged 76 in 2018 – proving that nothing is certain.

Environmental factors

It is possible that there are various triggers for the disease that affect our motor neurons.

Scientists are investigating whether a naturally occurring blue-green algae called cyanobacteria could be one of them.



The theory is that the toxin it produces could cause nerve damage or faulty proteins.

Other researchers are looking into whether metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic might be an issue.

These are toxins which are known to damage the brain.

Some studies have also found a possible link between smoking tobacco and MND.

None of this research has been conclusive. It is possible that none of these things has anything to do with the condition.



A spokesperson for MND said: “In short, the exact causes of motor neurone disease are currently not known.

“It is thought a number of genetic, environmental and lifestyle risk factors need to combine before most forms of MND develop.

“Together, these risk factors may ‘tip the balance’ towards someone developing the disease and identifying the factors and how they combine will help researchers discover why the disease starts and potentially find strategies to lower the risk.”

News.title: Shocking moment raging passenger SLAPS flight attendant after ‘accidentally bumping into each other’ on packed plane
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a passenger flies into a rage and slaps an air hostess in the face.

Flight attendant Ms Liu, 33, was completing her final safety checks when she accidentally bumped into Ms Zhang, 71, on a packed plane to Taiwan.





The elderly woman was incensed, first screaming at the baffled flight attendant before hitting the crew member in the face.

The outrageous incident occurred just before landing at 7PM on April 3.

The pilot had repeatedly cautioned passengers to sit down and fasten their seatbelts for touchdown.

But the zealous troublemaker could not be contained and stood up in the aisle to put her shoes on.



Ms Liu was walking down the plane completing final safety checks when she accidentally bumped into the disobedient passenger.

According to eye witnesses, she immediately apologised, and the elderly woman seemed not to mind before rapidly losing her temper.

The air hostess offered medical assistance, including ice packs, but her offer was refused.

Instead, the situation quickly escalated, culminating in the passenger slapping the flight attendant in the face.



Eye witnesses said that Ms Liu remained calm and professional despite the crazed behaviour of Ms Zhang.

The airline has banned the slap-happy fiend and placed her on a permanent no-fly list.

Upon landing, the authorities boarded the plane and apprehended Ms Zhang, and air hostess Ms Liu pressed assault charges against the disgraceful passenger.

Not to be beaten, the slap-happy fiend has also filed charges against the flight attendant, claiming that she was injured to her neck and right cheek.

It comes as another air stewardess was groped by a passenger mid-air on a flight to China.



Dramatic footage shows the perv passenger being dragged off the plane in disgrace.

He later protested that his actions did not “count as sexual harassment”.

News.title: Sudanese man, 27, arrested after four migrants died trying to board small boat crossing Channel
News.content:
CHANNEL TRAGEDY Sudanese man, 27, arrested after four migrants died trying to board small boat crossing Channel

A SUDANESE man has been arrested after four migrants died trying to cross the English Channel.

Two men and two women died off the coast of northern France on Thursday after being swept away by strong currents trying to board a dinghy.





The National Crime Agency said in a statement on Friday that a 27-year-old Sudanese man has been arrested on suspicion of endangering life.

He was put in cuffs on Friday morning following the deaths of four people whose identities have not yet been released.

The NCA added 38 people were returned to the French shore but 74 illegal migrants sailed on to the UK.

The suspect was arrested at Manston processing centre in Kent on suspicion of “endangering another during a journey by sea to the UK”.



He is in police custody and is being interviewed by NCA officers, who are also speaking to those who made the journey.

There is also an investigation led by French prosecutors into the circumstances that led to the launch of the boat – they are being assisted by the NCA.

Craig Turner, its deputy director, said: “Working with colleagues at home and abroad, we are determined to do all we can to identify and bring to justice those responsible for these four tragic deaths.”

Mike Tapp, the migration minister, added: “Every death in the Channel is a tragedy.



“Our experienced law enforcement teams will continue working relentlessly with international partners to prevent these perilous journeys and bring those responsible to justice.

“Through our Border Security Act, officers now have stronger powers to act earlier and disrupt, intercept and take down the operations of criminal smuggling gangs who bring illegal migrants to our shores.”

Francois-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, told reporters on Thursday that a small boat organised by people smugglers arrived on Équihen beach soon after 7am.

It had travelled up to the coast via a local canal, and aimed to pick up dozens of UK-bound migrants.

“We sadly have to report four deaths this morning,” Launch said at the time.



“The people who died were attempting to board a taxi-boat.

“I have to commend the actions of our officers and firefighters who, as you know, are deployed every day to stop these crossings.”

Speaking of the four people who died, he said: “They were already quite far into the sea.

“The currents, which can be dangerous here, swept them away.”



In the first two months of 2026, around 2,200 migrants crossed the Channel to the UK with about 41,500 crossing last year.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

On Tuesday, 137 arrived from France aboard two makeshift inflatables, bringing the total number this year to more than 5000.

It comes as a plan to allow British boats to intercept migrants at sea and return them to France has been firmly rejected by President Emmanuel Macron’s government.

News.title: Singer who collaborated with Professor Green left stranger with blood dripping down her face after nightclub attack
News.content:
CLUB ASSAULT Singer who collaborated with Professor Green left stranger with blood dripping down her face after nightclub attack

A SINGER who collaborated with Professor Green left a stranger with blood dripping down her face in a savage nightclub attack.

Natalie Pickthall, who performs under the name Nahli, hurled a cup at Eleanora Morgan at The Box Soho in London.





The “unprovoked” attack last July left the victim with a 2cm gash along her eyebrow.

Pickthall, 36, featured on rapper Professor Green’s 2019 song Bad Decisions and a track titled Catch 22 with presenter Big Narstie in 2020.

The performer, who was also previously part of girl group IV Rox, has now pleaded guilty to assault.



Westminster Magistrates’ Court heard victim Eleanora was on her way to smoking area of the club when she was approached by Pickthall’s ex-partner, who she did not know.

The hearing was told Pickthall then approached them and threw a drink in Eleanora’s face and chucked a glass which hit her on the eyebrow.

In a victim impact statement, dance teacher Eleanora said: “I felt the blood drip down my face.”

She also told how the attack had given her anxiety and made her feel as if she could no longer go out at night.



The court heard Pickthall, who appeared to wipe away tears as she sat in the dock, was arrested on a plane bound for Dubai after the assault.

Ms Onuchukwu, defending, said the assault was the result of a “split second decision” made “out of frustration” at an ex-partner.

She said that although the prosecution had described the object thrown as a “glass”, it was actually a “plastic cup”.

Pinkthall was sentenced to a community order consisting of a curfew requiring her to be at home in the UK between 9pm and 6am for four weeks.

The singer, who gave her address to the court as Essex but now lives in Dubai, was also ordered to pay £600 in compensation to the victim.

News.title: Terrifying moment distracted biker crosses tracks just as train speeds towards him in heartstopping near-tragedy
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a biker missed death by mere seconds as he drove into the path of an oncoming train.

The brazen biker ignored the lowered barriers, where other motorists were waiting, and ploughed ahead across the tracks in the city of Hanoi in Vietnam.





The man appeared almost nonchalant as he finished his call and rode into the crossing of a speeding commuter train.

He escaped death by mere inches as the train clipped the back of his motorbike, sending him flying into commuters waiting on the other side.

The law-abiding commuters were shocked and none too pleased to be struck by the reckless driver barrelling into them.



The clip shows two riders being felled by the flying man before getting up to shout at the distracted driver, with one kicking the side of the man’s motorbike in frustration.

CCTV footage showed that the man was on his phone seconds before riding into the crossfire of the huge railway train.

Hilariously, the reckless biker was also wearing a bright orange safety helmet.

It was not his garish safety gear which saved him however – but pure luck.



The man escaped by the skin of his teeth completely unhurt and walked away shaken, but alive.

It follows a horrifying near-miss as a motorbike skidded into the road and exploded into a fireball mere metres from two schoolchildren.

Doorbell footage captured the terrifying incident in which the bike flies through the air and hits a pole before bursting into flames.

The kids run for their lives away from the burning aftermath.

Also emerging from the flames was the rider – who was momentarily on fire.

News.title: Daniel Radcliffe admits to being 'sad and really scared' in drink and drugs battle
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Daniel Radcliffe admits to being 'sad and really scared' in drink and drugs battle

Daniel Radcliffe is currently captivating Broadway audiences with his one-person play Every Brilliant Thing. But while he is a famous actor to his fans, at home he is simply Dad

View 6 Images Tony-award-winning actor Daniel Radcliffe cut his cloth in the Harry Potter films (Image: Getty Images)

Captivating Broadway audiences with his one-person play Every Brilliant Thing, told through a list of every wonderful thing that makes life worth living, Daniel Radcliffe would top his own inventory with love. Every night, Tony winner Daniel, 36, asks five members of the audience to take a part in the interactive show - also handing out lines to other people to read, as he tackles subjects including suicide and depression.

‌



Playing schoolboy wizard Harry Potter in eight movies, aged 11 to 21, in his late teens, Daniel developed a drink problem as he struggled with fame - and identifies with some of the feelings. But, sober since 2013 - the year after meeting his partner, American actress Erin Darke on the set of Kill Your Darlings - and dad to their son, who is nearly three, Daniel is now flying high.

‌



He says: ”I have a long term sobriety. I am very grateful for that. I met my partner Erin 14 years ago. She has been a huge part of my happiness - and having a child. There is something about being truly known and understood by another human being. That is why love exists. You can’t emphasise how wonderful that is.”

‌



6 View 6 Images Daniel Radcliffe and Tom Felton pose during the NYC screening for the film "Merrily We Roll Along," based on the Broadway musical by Stephen Sondheim, at The Hudson Theatre on December 1, 2025 in New York City (Image: Bruce Glikas/WireImage) 6 View 6 Images Erin Darke and Daniel Radcliffe attend the The 77th Annual Tony Awards at David H. Koch Theater at Lincoln Center on June 16, 2024 in New York City. (Image: Getty Images for Tony Awards Pro)

And while he is a famous actor to his many fans, back home he is simply Dad - watching 101 Dalmatians with his son … on a loop. He says: “We have just watched The Little Mermaid. We are doing some nice early Disney. Right now I am just his dad and he has no idea what I do. He understands what policemen, doctors and firemen do. But acting? I tell him I help tell stories like from his book.”

Meanwhile, Every Brilliant Thing is a cathartic exercise for Daniel. He says: "There is something beautiful about doing this show. I am talking to people a lot at the stage door about issues too.” His latest role can also be a sobering experience when he spots A-list celebrities in the audience.

‌



He laughs: "I was trying to recruit a man in the audience to play a part in the show the other night. I looked to my right and Patti LuPone was sitting next to Susan Sarandon and she was sitting next to Jessica Laing. I was like ‘how cool and intimidating that all you three ladies hang out!’ We had Ian McKellen the other day and I was like ‘oh, cool. You are here...great! I’d better be good.’” Then, when he needed someone to high five during another performance, he picked out Anna Wintour, saying: “It is a memory I will take to my grave.”

Explaining the show’s unique format, he says: “I perform on stage with about five audience members and I hand out cards to about 35 people with words they say when I say a number. Someone also gets to throw confetti. It is very stressful, but it always comes together five minutes before we start It is awkward to find my love interest every night!”

6 View 6 Images Daniel Radcliffe and Erin Darke joined the picket line In New York City on July 21, 2023 in New York City. Members of SAG-AFTRA, Hollywood's largest union which represents actors and other media professionals, joined striking WGA (Writers Guild of America) workers in the first joint walkout against the studios since 1960 (Image: Getty Images) 6 View 6 Images Daniel Radcliffe appears in a scene from Warner Bros. Pictures' film "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Winning a Tony award for his role in the musical Merrily We Roll Along in 2024, his many stage, TV and movie credits include Equus, Swiss Army Man and Weird: The Al Yankovic Story and Miracle workers. But Daniel does not take his success for granted. He says: "There were moments in my late teens and early 20s when I was really sad, really scared. I did not know what the future would hold for me. I would have never believed then that I would experience the happiness that I am now, with my partner, my son and my life in general.”

Feeling in a strong position to advise young actors to deal with fame, he continues: "I met some of the Stranger Things kids recently. I say to them ‘do whatever the f*ck you want. You have done ‘the thing’. You now have the most amazing jumping off platform.’” He recalls the backlash he faced, aged 17, in a break from Harry Potter when he appeared nude on stage in the 2007 West End play Equus.

He says: “It was a very prestigious play. I was not damaging the [Potter] brand in any way. I remember once in the canteen where we were rehearsing someone left a newspaper open and the headline was "Crash. What is that? The sound of a career coming to a grinding halt.’ Looking around the room at amazing actors like Richard Griffiths, I thought ‘if I am screwing up, I could not be screwing-up with better people around me’.”

‌



For Daniel, a far bigger challenge than performing naked came when he had to sing and dance for the Broadway version of How To Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. He laughs: "Getting naked is easy. Dancing is the scariest thing I have ever done on stage, 100%. I said I could carry a tune but I will not dance. I told them there was zero chance. But they told me I had 18 months and I had to do dance classes. I guess we made it happen, but I want to put it out there - I can’t dance.”

View 6 Images Daniel Radcliffe during a photocall for the theatre production of Equus in 2012 (Image: PA)

Still, the part landed him his Tony award-winning role as Charley Kringas in Merrily We Roll Along. Today, he’s appearing on Broadway alongside a rival show starring his old Hogwarts foe Tom Felton, who has reprised his role as Draco Malfoy in a stage adaptation of Harry Potter And The Cursed Child. Daniel says: "It is surreal to see Tom on a billboard now in Times Square. We met before we were teenagers in Watford doing Potter and we grew up doing all sorts of stuff we should not have been doing. But now, to be both on Broadway at the same time is lovely.”

‌



Daniel appreciates his lucky start in the Potter films, which has helped him amass a fortune reputed to be close to £100million, but still finds it hard to watch them. He says: "I guess I have more time now for me in the early films. When I was 18 I would cringe watching the early ones. Now I think the early films are sweet and I cringe watching myself when I was 18.”

His next role will see him tackle the subject of homosexuality in the military in the Vietnam War. Meanwhile, he is keen to keep his son - whose name he will not disclose - out of the spotlight for as long as possible - although he says he’s starting to get an inkling that his dad is on TV. He says: "We were watching the [winter) Olympics recently and an ad for my new TV show popped up. I had left the room and I popped up on the screen and my son went ‘Dada’ in the tone of ‘I am not crazy, right?’ A bunch of kids in our building saw it too and one five-year-old said ‘I saw you on TV. What were you doing there?’ All I can do is be his uncool, very unimpressive dad for as long as I can. That is the goal."

*Daniel Radcliffe stars in Every Brilliant Thing at the Hudson Theatre, New York until May 24.

News.title: UK snow maps reveal 12 major cities face flurries on Saturday – see full list
News.content:
UK snow maps reveal 12 major cities face flurries on Saturday – see full list

Surprise snow is on the cards on Saturday as weather forecasting maps suggest as many as 12 major cities across the UK could see some unseasonal wintry flurries

View 4 Images Snow is expected in Scotland before moving southward throughout Saturday morning (Image: WXCHARTS)

Advanced weather modelling maps suggest Brits in several cities could face snow this weekend.

‌



The GFS model shows a weather front moving in from the Atlantic in the early hours of Saturday morning, initially bringing rain to Wales and the south-west. This precipitation is expected to fall as snow over Scotland to begin with, but areas further south could also see wintry showers as the morning progresses.

‌



Maps for 6am show snow falling across a massive swathe of Wales as well as north-west of England and parts of Scotland. Some flurries might even reach the south-west of England.

‌



While by 9am, purple areas on the maps show snow also falling in the Midlands and the north-east of England. Throughout this spell tomorrow morning, the data suggests at least 12 major cities could see some of the white stuff.

View 4 Images Further snow is expected at 9am on Saturday (Image: WXCHARTS)

Snow coverage maps show most of Scotland, northern England and Wales could see some flakes settle on the ground. However, the data suggests accumulations will not be greater than 1cm, apart from over hills in Scotland.

The Met Office expects temperatures to peak at 15C tomorrow in southern areas, a far cry from the blazing 26C heat we experienced earlier this week.

‌



The Met Office forecast for Saturday states: “Rain across central and western areas, but clearing eastwards. Showers follow, heavy in Northern Ireland and western Scotland. Windy with coastal gales in the west. Temperatures near seasonal average.”

View 4 Images A large chunk of the UK could see some snow settled on the ground (Image: WXCHARTS)

BBC Weather says tomorrow will start cloudy with a risk of showers in western parts of the UK. Its forecast states: “Tomorrow will start mostly cloudy, with rain reaching the south-east, and showers in the west. In the afternoon, the risk of showers will persist but some sunny spells will develop. Windy in the west.

Article continues below

“Sunday will be breezy with sunny spells and showers, these most frequent in the north and the west. Some of the showers could turn thundery in the afternoon.

“On Monday, winds will ease, but there will be a mix of sunshine and showers, these mainly in the north. Tuesday looks to be mostly dry before some rain reaches Northern Ireland by evening.”

News.title: 'Perilous' return to earth for Artemis crew - fireball risk, 'anxious' officials, flaw on ship
News.content:
'Perilous' return to earth for Artemis crew - fireball risk, 'anxious' officials, flaw on ship

The Artemis II crew are preparing for re-entry back to earth, after travelling further away from our home planet than anyone ever has before - but getting home is itself filled with danger

View 5 Images The four-person Artemis II crew have been a long way from home, but their facing their most dangerous challenge yet (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The Artemis II crew are about to face the most dangerous part of their mission, getting home.

‌



The world has watched captivated as four astronauts ventured further away from planet Earth than anyone has ever managed before - with photos and video clips from their voyage into space sweeping across the internet. After breaking records and inspiring people the world over, NASA's Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman, and Christina Koch, as well as Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, are heading home.

‌



One exceptionally memorable moment during the daring journey saw the crew name a "bright spot" crater after Commander Reid Wiseman's late wife, Carroll Taylor Wiseman, who died from cancer back in 2020 - giving new meaning to the often uttered phrase, 'love you to the moon and back'. "We all pretty much broke down right there," Wiseman has reportedly said, adding it was the "pinnacle" of the adventure for him.

‌



WATCH Artemis II's re-entry live on the Mirror Blog

But now after preparing for years and conducting their mission, it's time for the four strong crew of highly trained astronauts to return home - which might be one of the biggest challenges yet. Due to arrive back home, in the early hours of Saturday morning, safely managing their splash landing in the ocean off the coastline of San Diego is no mean feat, with officials "anxious" about the process that will see their craft turn into a "fireball" as it re-enters the Earth's atmosphere at speeds up to 23,839 mph, this is 40 times the speed of a normal airplane flight.

View 5 Images The crew are heading home on board the Orion spacecraft (Image: NASA)

‌



As the Orion capsule heads home, it has to go through three trajectory correction burns - this is where it fires up its thrusters to ensure it's exactly on the correct route path home and crucially that it's moving at the perfect speed required for the trip. The final burn happens just five hours before the big moment of re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere.

Before they reach this point though, the astronauts need to don their spacesuits inside the crew module, which will break away from the service module - this part of the capsule contains the engines that have moved the craft through space, and will burn in the atmosphere, so it isn't coming with them.

About 76 miles from the surface of the Earth, things start heating up - literally. Plasma that is incredibly hot will in just seconds "build up" around their craft because of the friction caused by the atmosphere and temperatures can reach up to 1600 degrees celsius. The crew will be kept safe from these super-high temperatures through a heat shield that has been exposed ahead of time, but during these moments all communications with NASA will be totally blocked by the plasma.

‌



View 5 Images Mission specialist Christina Koch looking back at earth through the window of the Orion spacecraft (Image: NASA/AFP via Getty Images)

However, during in the uncrewed first Artemis mission back in 2022, "chunks came off" of the heat shield and it "cracked" reports The Sun. Luckily the craft in that test did make it back to earth, so NASA ruled it was safe for use on this mission. Based on the test flight, the space agency has made some alterations to the route home, ensuring that the moment of re-entry into the atmosphere is as short as possible, but the crew will be coming back at a higher speed.

The heat shield is completely crucial to the astronaut's safe return, so the prospect of it not operating perfectly keeps one NASA administrator "up at night" because there is "no plan B". Jared Isaacman has explained: "In terms of what keeps me up at night, my blood pressure will be elevated until they're under parachutes in the water off the West Coast.

‌



"There's no plan B there. That is the thermal protection system. The heat shield has to work."

View 5 Images The record-breaking four person crew (Image: SIPA/Shutterstock)

However one heat shield expert has issued a stark warning about the system and the "serious risk" associated with it. "The technical and organisational issues associated with the Orion heat shield represent a serious risk. History shows accidents occur when organisations convince themselves they understand problems they do not. This issue exhibits the same patterns that preceded past catastrophes," said former astronaut and NASA engineer Charlie Camarda.

‌



After getting through the extreme heat at the re-entry point, the cover has to fall away from the crew module to allow their speed to slow and for the parachutes that do this to work properly. There are two parachutes - 23 feet in width - that will help the slow down the velocity, and they are deployed at 25,000 feet, hopefully getting the module down to 307 miles per hour.

In a carefully planned and choreographed procedure, three smaller parachutes come into play at about 9,500 feet which pull out the main parachutes that do the work of slowing things down even further - these final three are huge at 115 foot wide - and they will help the capsule get down to just 17mph from 130mph so they can splashdown safely.

Amit Kshatriya - NASA associate administrator - has said they are "confident" this will all work out as planned, but adds, "The crew has done their part, now we have to do ours," with the four astronaut's lives in their hands. "Every system we've demonstrated over the past nine days - life support, navigation, propulsion, communications - all of it depends on the final minutes of flight," he said, per Sky News.

‌



"We have high confidence in the system and the heat shield and the parachutes and the recovery systems we put together. The engineering supports it. The Artemis I flight data supports it. All of our ground test supports it, our analysis supports it."

View 5 Images The historic 10-day mission is coming to an end (Image: BEST IMAGE / BACKGRID)

However, Kshatriya is feeling "anxious" no matter how well prepared they are. "There's no question that I'll be anxious," he has said. "But we'll be with the families. We'll be with them. We'll all be together. I have full confidence in the team."

‌



He continues, "it's impossible to say you don't have irrational fears left...But I would tell you I don't have any rational fears about what's going to happen."

Pilot of the Artemis II mission Victor Glover admitted recently that the prospect of the "fireball" return has been on his mind since the very moment it was confirmed he and his crew would be undertaking the long journey into space and home again. "I've actually been thinking about entry since 3 April, 2023, when we got assigned to this mission," he said during their 10-day record-breaking mission.

"There are so many more pictures and stories, and I haven't even begun to process what we've been through. We've still got two more days, and riding a fireball through the atmosphere is profound as well."

News.title: Kamala Harris confirms whether she's considering running for President again
News.content:
Kamala Harris confirms whether she's considering running for President again

She was asked about her plans for the future by TV host Rev Al Sharpton at a civil rights convention - and she gave her firmest answer yet

View Image She gave her firmest answer yet on whether she'd have a third run for the Oval Office (Image: Kyle Stevens/Shutterstock)

Kamala Harris says she's "thinking about" running for President again, she has confirmed today.

‌



She was asked about her plans for the future by TV host Rev Al Sharpton at a civil rights convention.

‌



"I might," she said. "I'm thinking about it. But let me also say this. I served for four years being a heartbeat away from the PResidency of the United States. I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office. I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room.

‌



"I know what the job is. And I knwo what it requires. I also know - one of the things I've been doing is travelling the country in the last year, and the one thing I'm really clear about is the status quo is not working and hasn’t been working for a lot of people for a long time."

It's her strongest indication yet that she's planning to stand to be the Democrat candidate in the 2028 Presidential election. She lost the election in 2024 to Donald Trump, after replacing former President Joe Biden on the ticket late in the campaign.

‌



While she's still considered an outsider to win in 2028 by bookmakers, she continues to poll the highest out of any Democrat candidate in most national polls - beating her next nearest rival, California Governor Gavin Newsom by more than seven points in an average of polls.

She first indicated a third run for the Oval Office was a possibility in an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg last year, saying: ""I am not done. I have lived my entire career as a life of service and it's in my bones."

News.title: Girl, 13, killed in Corby after e-bike incident 'lived life to fullest'
News.content:
Girl, 13, killed in Corby after e-bike incident 'lived life to fullest'

Ella Walden, aged 13, tragically died after suffering serious injuries from falling off an e-bike on Elizabeth Street in Corby, with her family saying their lives 'will never be complete again'

View 2 Images The family of Ella Walden have paid tribute to her (Image: PA)

The family of a 13-year-old girl who died in an e-bike accident in Corby have told how she "lived life to the fullest".

‌



Ella Walden died following an incident in the town’s Elizabeth Street involving an e-bike. The teenager suffered serious injuries when she fell off the e-bike on Elizabeth Street. She was rushed to hospital and later tragically died.

‌



The incident took place between 2pm and 3pm on April 7 and police are now keen to hear from anyone who may have witnessed what happened or have footage. A 32-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of perverting the course of justice and road traffic offences over the incident and has been bailed.

‌



View 2 Images Ella Walden was taken to hospital but sadly died (Image: PA)

Now, her family have penned a tribute, which was shared by Northamptonshire Police, stating how their lives ' will never be complete again'.

It read: “Our lives will never be complete again after losing our beautiful Ella. She was the most amazing, strong-willed, feisty girl, with the most precious smile. Ella had an infectious personality and could light up even the emptiest room. She made a lasting impression on everyone she met, and you could hear her before you saw her, so life is so quiet without her.

‌



“As a family, we were the lucky ones to have her as ours, but she has been taken from us far too soon. Ella was incredibly loyal and always stood up for what she believed in. She had a kind heart and was always there for anyone who was struggling. “Ella loved being in the limelight and truly excelled in drama - she was never happier than when she was performing. She lived life to the fullest. To the world she was Ella, but to us she was the world. Life will forever have an empty space without her, but her memory will live on with us all forever.”

Police said this morning: "Detectives from Northamptonshire Police’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit have arrested a man in connection with an incident which led to the death of a girl in Corby.

"The incident happened on Tuesday, April 7, between 2pm and 3pm, when the girl suffered serious injuries after falling off an e-bike in the town’s Elizabeth Street. She was taken to hospital but sadly died a short time later.

Article continues below

"Now, a 32-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of perverting the course of justice and road traffic offences, in connection with the incident. He has been released on police bail pending further enquiries.

"Officers would still like to hear from anyone who may have witnessed the incident or who may have CCTV or dash-cam footage of the collision.

"Anyone with information is asked to email CollisionAppeals@northants.police.uk or call the Drivewatch Hotline on 0800 174615, or Northamptonshire Police on 101. Please quote incident number 26000198505 when passing on any information to make sure it gets to the right person as quickly as possible."

News.title: Prince Harry sued for defamation by Sentebale charity he co-founded
News.content:
Prince Harry sued for defamation by Sentebale charity he co-founded

Court documents have shown that Prince Harry is being sued for defamation by the Sentebale charity he co-founded in honour of his late mother Princess Diana

View 4 Images Prince Harry is being sued by the Sentebale charity (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Prince Harry's long-running dispute with the charity he helped set up in honour of his late mother before quitting has taken a dramatic new turn.

It has emerged that the Duke of Sussex is being sued for defamation by Sentebale, which he co-founded in 2006 to help support young people living with HIV and AIDS in Lesotho and Botswana. Last year, Harry and co-founder Prince Seeiso of Lesotho stepped down as its patrons in support of a group of trustees, who resigned following a bitter boardroom battle with charity chairwoman Sophie Chandauka.

Now, online High Court filings show that Harry is a defendant in a libel or slander claim alongside Mark Dyer, a former trustee. No documents are currently available in the claim originally filed on March 24.

View 4 Images Harry with Sentebale chair Sophie Chandauka (Image: PA)

Sentebale, which means forget-me-not, was thrown into crisis last March, when Harry and Prince Seeiso appeared to suddenly step down as patrons.

It came after the charity's trustees sought to introduce a new fundraising strategy, with the dispute arising between Ms Chandauka and some of the trustees and Harry.

A war of words followed the resignations with Harry and Seeiso issuing a joint statement in March 2025, describing their decision as “unthinkable”, adding the trustees “acted in the best interest of the charity in asking the chair to step down” while “in turn, she sued the charity to remain in this voluntary position, further underscoring the broken relationship”.

Chandauka hit back in a television interview, accusing the duke of being “involved” in a “cover-up” of an investigation about bullying, harassment and misogyny at the organisation and said the “toxicity” of his brand had impacted the charity, which she claimed had seen a drop in donors since Harry moved to the US.

View 4 Images Harry quit as patron of Sentebale last year (Image: Getty Images for Sentebale)

Later, it was claimed Harry sent an 'unpleasant text' to Ms Chandauka after she failed to publicly quash rumours of a rift with his wife, Meghan.

The charity chair claimed that after an awkward moment between her and Meghan was captured on camera at a polo match to raise funds for Sentebale in Florida in 2024, she was asked to issue a statement by Harry's team defending the duchess.

She said she refused the request saying, "We cannot become an extension of the Sussex machine". It was then reported that Harry sent her a direct message asking her to "explain herself", using "imperious" language and leaving the charity chair "taken aback".

A probe by the Charity Commission followed after Ms Chanduaka reported the prince and the trustees to the regulator over alleged bullying and harassment.

View 4 Images Harry in Lesotho in 2006, when he helped to launch the charity (Image: PA)

Its report criticised all parties in the dispute for allowing it to play out publicly and described how all trustees contributed to a “missed opportunity” to resolve the issues that led to the serious disagreement, which risked undermining public trust in charities generally.

The regulator, which cannot investigate individual allegations of bullying, found no evidence of systemic bullying or harassment, including misogyny or misogynoir at the charity, but acknowledged “the strong perception of ill treatment” felt by some involved.

A source at the time said that Harry had been left emotionally devastated by the events, after 19 years of working with the charity. A spokesperson for Harry at the time took aim at Chandauka saying: "The report falls troublingly short in many regards, primarily the fact that the consequences of the current Chair’s actions will not be borne by her, but by the children who rely on Sentebale’s support."

Article continues below

Chandauka vowed to honour the founding mission of the charity Sentebale, and said: "The unexpected adverse media campaign that was launched by those who resigned on 24 March 2025 has caused incalculable damage and offers a glimpse of the unacceptable behaviours displayed in private. We are emerging not just grateful to have survived, but stronger: more focused, better governed, boldly ambitious and with our dignity intact.

"Despite the recent turbulence, we will always be inspired by the vision of our founders, Prince Harry and Prince Seeiso, who established Sentebale in memory of their precious mothers, Princess Diana and Queen ‘Mamohato. To all who believe in our mission: please walk with us as Sentebale recovers, renews, and rises to meet the hopes and expectations of the next generation."

News.title: Queen Elizabeth II nearly left out iconic line from historic Covid lockdown speech
News.content:
Queen Elizabeth II nearly left out iconic line from historic Covid lockdown speech

A new book claims that the late Queen Elizabeth II had to be persuaded to included a line from a famous wartime song in her address to the nation during the Covid lockdown in 2020

View 4 Images Queen Elizabeth II addressed the nation earlier to calm fears over the spread of the coronavirus pandemic in April 2020 (Image: BUCKINGHAM PALACE/AFP via Getty)

Queen Elizabeth II had to be persuaded to include the famous ‘We’ll meet again’ line in her historic address to the nation during the coronavirus lockdown.

‌



The late monarch issued a heartfelt rallying cry in a bid to unite the nation during the outbreak of the Covid pandemic, invoking the wartime spirit of Dame Vera Lynn. Drawing on her experience during the Blitz, she praised NHS staff battling the deadly outbreak and urged the public to play its part by staying home.

‌



As the UK death rate rose to nearly 5,000 in the early days of the pandemic, the Queen said: “We will succeed, and that success will belong to every one of us. Many will feel a painful sense of separation. Better days will return. We'll meet again.”

‌



View 4 Images Queen Elizabeth II addressed the nation earlier to calm fears over the spread of the coronavirus pandemic in April 2020 (Image: BUCKINGHAM PALACE/AFP via Getty)

In just her fifth address to the nation during her incredible 70-year reign, it will be remembered as one of her most powerful. But a new book by royal biographer Robert Hardman suggests that the Queen nearly struck out the line, believing it to be too “whimsical”.

‌



In his new book, Elizabeth II: In Private. In Public. The Inside Story, Hardman says that the Queen’s private secretary, Sir Edward Young, had initially proposed to the Queen that she should include the line from the popular song of the Second World War.

It was included in several drafts delivered to Her Majesty including her daily red box of government paperwork. Yet the royal aide found it had been crossed out by the Queen.

Hardman writes: “Eventually, he pressed the point in person and the Queen finally agreed. So it was that she ended her address with echoes of Vera Lynn’s great wartime refrain: ‘Better days will return; we will be with our friends again; we will meet again.”

‌



View 4 Images An image of Queen Elizabeth II and quotes from her broadcast in relation to the coronavirus epidemic are displayed on lights in London's Piccadilly Circus (Image: PA)

The eventual inclusion, delivered by the Queen on April 5, 2020 from Windsor Castle where she had gone to stay after being evacuated from Buckingham Palace, became the focal point for news bulletins and was splashed on the front pages of newspapers around the world.

In the new biography, Hardman also writes how the Queen was also worried about Princess Anne - frequently dubbed the monarchy’s “hardest working royal” - when the yearly list of engagements are totted up, was worried about her daughter exerting herself.

Article continues below

View 4 Images Princess Anne was a great support to her mother, the Queen, especially during the covid pandemic (Image: ITV)

The Princess Royal appeared to be a great comfort to her mother during the covid lockdowns, taking part in video calls with her to speak to charities and organisations they were both involved in as part of the Queen’s mantra, “one must be seen to be believed”.

“The Queen was always very worried about Anne working too hard,” a former member of staff told Hardman. “She always wanted to know where her children were. ‘Where’s Edward today?’ And so on, but she would often say, ‘Anne’s travelling everywhere, and she works so hard, and I’ve got to tell her to slow down.’”

News.title: Donald Trump says US ships are 'reloading' in case peace talks go badly in 24 hours
News.content:
Donald Trump says US ships are 'reloading' in case peace talks go badly in 24 hours

He said he'd know whether peace talks were going to be successful "in about 24 hours" - after crowing on Truth Social about the "world's most powerful reset" of America's military presence in the region

View 2 Images Trump, who has not been seen in public since Monday, said US forces are "resetting" (Image: AP)

Donald Trump says the US is reloading warships ready to resume strikes against Iran if peace talks fail.

‌



"We're going to find out in about 24 hours. We're going to know soon," he told the New York Post, when asked if he thought tomorrow's talks in Islamabad, Pakistan would be successful.

‌



The interview follows a cryptic Truth Social post where Trump wrote: "WORLD'S MOST POWERFUL RESET!!!"

‌



"We have a reset going," Trump said. "We're loading up the ships with the best ammunition, the best weapons ever made - even better than what we did previously and we blew them apart."

He went on: "But we're loading up the ships. We're loading up the ships with the best weapons ever made, even at a higher level than we use to do a complete decimation.

"And if we don't have a deal, we will be using them, and we will be using them very effectively."

‌



With the ceasefire in Iran still shaky, Vice President JD Vance headed Friday to Pakistan for high-level talks with Iranian officials, as Israel and Hezbollah traded fire and Tehran maintained its stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz.

Many issues could derail the truce and the negotiations aimed at making a broader deal to stop the fighting permanently.

Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency, close to the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, claimed that the talks set for Saturday would not happen unless Israel stopped its attacks in Lebanon. And Trump complained that Iran was “doing a very poor job” by not allowing the free flow of ships through the strait, through which 20% of the world ’s traded oil once passed.

‌



Kuwait, meanwhile, said it was targeted by seven drone attacks since Thursday that it blamed on Iran and its militia allies in the region. Though the Guard denied launching any assault, it has carried out attacks across the Mideast in the past that it did not claim.

Preparations for the talks between Iran and the US appeared to be moving forward, with Vance boarding Air Force Two for the long flight to Islamabad.

Elsewhere, negotiations between Israel and Lebanon were expected to begin next week in the US capital, according to a US official and a person familiar with the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the delicacy of the matter.

‌



Before his departure, Vance said he believes negotiation with Iran will be “positive.”

But he added, “If they’re going to try and play us, then they’re going to find that the negotiating team is not that receptive.”

In Islamabad, security forces locked down key parts of the Pakistani capital, erecting barricades along routes from the airport to the city before the delegations arrived.

‌



Israel and Lebanon will have direct negotiations

Israel’s insistence that the ceasefire in Iran does not include a pause in its fighting with Hezbollah has threatened to sink the deal. The militant group joined the war in support of its backer, Iran.

The day the truce was announced, Israel pounded Beirut with airstrikes, killing more than 300 people, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry. It was the deadliest day in the country since the war began Feb. 28. On Friday, Lebanon’s state-run new agency said Israeli warplanes struck near a state security office in the southern town of Nabatieh, killing eight officers.

‌



Trump said Thursday that he has asked Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to dial back the strikes. Early Friday, Israel’s military said it hit approximately 10 launchers in Lebanon that had fired rockets toward northern Israel a day earlier.

Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, warned that continued Israeli attacks on Hezbollah would bring “explicit costs and STRONG responses.”

Also Thursday, Netanyahu said he authorized the negotiations with Lebanon “as soon as possible” with the aim of disarming Hezbollah militants and establishing relations between the neighbors, which have technically been at war since Israel was established in 1948.

‌



The Lebanese government did not respond.

In a first statement since Israel announced direct negotiations with Lebanon, Hezbollah chief Naim Kassem urged Lebanese officials to stop offering “free concessions,” but he did not take a clear stance on the talks.

Two days after Israel's intense barrage, people sifted through the wreckage of their homes, trying to salvage furniture and personal mementos. Some expressed gratitude that they did not lose loved ones.

‌



“There is no substitute for family,” said Wissam Tabila, 35. “Everything else can be replaced.”

Strait of Hormuz remains a sticking point

Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has sent oil prices skyrocketing, driven stocks down and roiled the world economy. Tehran's control over the waterway has proved its biggest strategic advantage in the war.

‌



The spot price of Brent crude, the international standard, was around $97 Friday, up more than 30% since the war started.

Before the conflict, over 100 ships passed through the strait each day — many carrying oil to Asia. With the ceasefire in place, only 12 have been recorded passing through.

Trump complained about that situation, writing on his social media platform: “Iran is doing a very poor job, dishonorable some would say, of allowing Oil to go through the Strait of Hormuz.”

‌



“That is not the agreement we have!” Trump wrote of the trickle of ships Iran has allowed to pass.

Questions also remain over the fate of Iran’s missile and nuclear programs, which the U.S. and Israel sought to eliminate in going to war.

The US insists Iran must never be able to build nuclear weapons and wants to remove Tehran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, which could be used to make them. Iran insists its program is peaceful.

‌



View 2 Images (Image: AP)

Trump has said that the US would work with Iran to remove the uranium, though Tehran has not confirmed that.

More than 3,000 people have been killed in Iran, a top Iranian officer told the state-run Iran newspaper. Iran’s government has not provided any definitive death toll from the war.

Article continues below

In Lebanon, more than 1,888 people have been killed and 1 million have been displaced. Over a dozen people have died in Gulf Arab states and the occupied West Bank, while 23 civilians were killed in Israel. Thirteen U.S. service members have been killed.

In other developments, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces shot down Iranian‑designed Shahed drones in several Middle Eastern countries during the Iran war. The missions, carried out with domestically produced interceptor drones, were part of efforts to help partners counter the same weapons Russia uses in Ukraine, he said.

News.title: LeBron and Bronny James record first son-to-father assist in NBA history

News.title: Gold Dancer put down after winning at Aintree
News.content:
Gold Dancer had to be put down after suffering a broken back when winning the Mildmay Novices' Chase on day two of the Grand National Meeting at Aintree.

The horse dragged his back legs through the final fence when leading Regent's Stroll and was ridden out to win by four lengths under Paul Townend for trainer Willie Mullins.

Gold Dancer was immediately pulled up after crossing the finish line, with Townend dismounting and screens erected for veterinary experts to assess and treat the horse but the seven-year-old was put down.

Owners Gigginstown said: "He's been put down. He broke his back. It's terribly sad for the horse.

"What could Paul Townend do? He felt fine, it was just when he pulled up that something was wrong."

Emma Slawinski, chief executive at the League Against Cruel Sports, said: "Year after year we see horses dying at Aintree for people's entertainment and a cheap bet. Sadly, Gold Dancer is the latest victim of this heartless spectacle, which flies in the face of animal welfare.

"The public and businesses should boycott the Aintree Festival, refuse to bet on the racing, and stop watching the ITV coverage and advertising which glosses over the animal cruelty.

"The government needs to act as the British Horseracing Authority and Jockey Club is prioritising gambling profits over the lives of the horses."

James Given, director of equine health and welfare for the British Horseracing Authority, said: "The horse jumped and slipped and lost his back end.

"He came up very quickly and took one half stride to get organised and galloped away.

"I was in the inquiry and gave evidence that looked into the incident - I was able to watch front on and behind - and the horse stayed as straight as an arrow and wasn't deviating off a straight line or being asymmetric, the back legs were following the front legs exactly.

"It was only when they went past the finishing line that he turned around to the left as the track goes and went from cantering to a trot and the action changed and Paul [Townend] became aware.

"He immediately jumped off and was attended by the vets. I don't believe Paul was able to notice that injury at all.

"He would have felt nothing but normal to him and it was only from the action from a canter to a trot he became aware and acted exactly as he should have done."

Two horses, Willy De Houelle and Celebre D'Allen, died at last year's Aintree Festival.

A charity co-founded by Prince Harry in honour of his late mother, Princess Diana, is suing the British royal for libel at the High Court in London, court records revealed on Friday.

Sentebale, established by the Duke of Sussex, King Charles’s younger son, in 2006, have launched defamation action against Harry, alleging “co-ordinated adverse media campaign” which caused “operational disruption and reputational harm”, its board of trustees said.

Sentebale lodged the defamation claim last month against Harry and his close friend Mark Dyer, who was also a trustee of the organisation.

The charity was launched in 2006 to support young people with HIV and AIDS in Lesotho and Botswana.

Harry resigned as a patron in March 2025 after a public falling-out with its board chair, Sophie Chandauka.

The charity's co-founder Prince Seeiso of Lesotho and the board of trustees joined Harry in leaving Sentebale, which he helped set up nine years after Diana was killed in a Paris car crash and which means "forget-me-not" in the local language of Lesotho in southern Africa.

The 41-year-old prince called the breakdown in the relationship with Chandauka devastating, while she reported him and the trustees to Britain's charity regulator for alleged bullying and harassment.

open image in gallery Sentebale chairwoman Sophie Chandauka ( Sky News )

Dr Sophie Chandauka previously said Harry’s “unleashing of the Sussex machine” had broken the relationship between the prince and the 540 people who work for the Sentebale charity.

She claimed the Duke briefed the press about stepping back from the charity before letting her or the charity’s executive director know first.

“The only reason I’m here... is because at some point on Tuesday, Prince Harry authorised the release of a damaging piece of news to the outside world without informing me or my country directors, or my executive director,” Dr Chandauka said on Sky’s Sunday Morning with Trevor Phillips in March last year.

Adding: “And can you imagine what that attack has done for me, on me and the 540 individuals in the Sentebale organisations and their family?

“That is an example of harassment and bullying at scale.”

After a review, the Charity Commission reported it had found no evidence of bullying, but said there had been weak governance and criticised all parties for allowing an internal dispute to become public.

In a statement, its board of trustees and executive director said: “Sentebale has commenced legal proceedings in the High Court of England and Wales.

“The charity seeks the court’s intervention, protection and restitution following a co-ordinated adverse media campaign conducted since March 25 2025 that has caused operational disruption and reputational harm to the charity, its leadership and its strategic partners.

open image in gallery Harry resigned as a patron in March 2025 after a public falling-out with its board chair, Sophie Chandauka. ( AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth, File )

“The proceedings have been brought against Prince Harry and Mark Dyer, identified through evidence as the architects of that adverse media campaign, which has had significant viral impact and triggered an onslaught of cyber-bullying directed at the charity and its leadership.

“Sentebale has experienced the adverse media campaign as false narratives circulated through the media about the charity and its leadership, attempts to undermine its relationships with staff, existing and prospective partners, and the forced diversion of leadership time and resources into managing a reputational crisis not of the charity’s making.”

The legal action was “necessary and important”, Sentebale’s board of trustees said.

The statement added: “Sentebale’s development sector funders have maintained 100% of their financial commitment throughout this period and the charity has been deeply moved by the continued generosity of individual donors who have stood firm alongside them.

“The commitment of our partners and donors reflects a shared conviction that good governance is fundamental to the integrity of any charitable organisation, and their faith in the continued work of the charity. It is also a reflection of the resolve of the board and the teams in Lesotho and Botswana who have remained resilient and focused on the work in the face of sustained pressure.

“At a time when international aid is contracting and the needs of children across southern Africa are growing, the work Sentebale delivers for 78,000 young lives is increasingly critical.

“The charity should not continue to use its resources to manage and address the damage this adverse media campaign has caused to its operations and partnerships. This must stop.

“The board and executive director have taken this legal action to secure that protection. The costs of doing so are met entirely by external funding and no charitable funds have been used.

“The board and executive director trust that those who believe in Sentebale’s mission will understand why this legal action, whilst difficult, was necessary and important, and will continue to stand with us as we focus on the work ahead.

“Sentebale’s focus remains where it has always been: the children and young people of Lesotho and Botswana.

“Sentebale does not intend to comment further on this matter while legal proceedings are ongoing.”

Marine heat waves are supercharging damage caused by hurricanes and tropical cyclones across the globe, a new study found.

Researchers looked at 1,600 tropical cyclones — the broader category of storms that includes hurricanes — that made landfall since 1981 and found those that went over the extra-hot water were more likely to intensify rapidly, a problem that's becoming more frequent. This resulted in 60% more disasters that caused at least $1 billion in damage — adjusted for inflation — when they hit land, according to a study in Friday's journal Science Advances.

A better understanding of how marine heat waves amplify hurricanes could help forecasters, emergency officials and long-term planners prepare for future storms.

The study defined marine heat waves as long-lasting, large areas of water in the top 10% of historical heat. They are becoming more of a danger with climate change and ever hotter oceans, study authors said. Warm water is fuel for hurricanes.

“These marine heat waves affect more than half of landfalling tropical cyclones,'' said study co-author Gregory Foltz, an oceanographer at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “They're happening closer to land and more frequently, so I think people need to pay attention and know that these are more likely to result in extreme damages when they make landfall.”

It's important for meteorologists forecasting the storm track to see if these hurricanes go over a marine heat wave because it is more likely to intensify rapidly which “can potentially have a bigger impact on landfall,” Foltz said.

Just look at damaging hurricanes that smacked the United States in 2023, said study co-author Hamed Moftakhari, a coastal engineering professor who studies compound hazards at the University of Alabama.

“The story of Helene and Milton is that if you've got a warmer ocean, you've got the fuel to supercharge tropical cyclones even in a cascade. So within a few weeks you could get two rapidly intensified hurricanes making landfall in the west coast of Florida,” Moftakhari said. “This is shocking but should also be alarming for people.”

The study also points to October 2023's Hurricane Otis, which rapidly intensified from a tropical storm to a top level Category 5 hurricane in one day, then caused about $16 billion in damage and 52 deaths when it made landfall near Acapulco, Mexico, with 165 mph (265 kph) winds.

Researchers said the higher damage, compared with storms that didn’t cross marine heat waves, wasn’t driven by increased coastal development. Storms that crossed hot water and hit developed coasts were contrasted with other storms that hit similarly urbanized areas but without crossing hot water, said study lead author Soheil Radfar, a scientist who does hurricane hazard modeling at Princeton University.

Science has long known that warm water fuels and often strengthens tropical cyclones, providing more of a link on causation.

That means the future looks more dangerous, Radfar said.

“All these pieces of the puzzle are going to be really challenging for the coastal environment in the next four decades when you have more rapid intensification, more marine heat waves," Radfar said. This “is going to be really costly and frightening for the coastline environment, and it’s going to cause more billion-dollar disasters in the future.”

Moftakhari said “from a coastal engineering and risk management perspective, this has important implications for how governments plan, design, and respond to these hazards.”

Evacuation planning must account for storms that cross ocean hot spots being more likely to intensify rapidly and pose greater threats, according to Moftakhari. Earlier warnings and triggers on when people leave may be needed when there are marine heat waves. Designs for flood protection, drainage system, sea walls all have to be updated to the new worsening storm reality, he said.

Outside scientists said the study fits with the known physics of hurricanes and climate change, while putting a more specific number on the likelihood for mega-damage when marine heat waves are present.

“Climate change is causing stronger and longer-duration marine heat waves. Tropical cyclones draw their energy and produce heavy rain via evaporation from warm ocean waters,” said University at Albany atmospheric sciences professor Brian Tang, who wasn't part of the study. “It’s reasonable that marine heat waves are turbocharging hurricanes, provided other environmental conditions are favorable for hurricanes to intensify. In effect, the dice is being loaded.”

News.title: I’m a philosopher. I’m convinced that Trump isn’t lying − he’s doing something worse
News.content:
